data.title: Chronic inhibition of mTOR by rapamycin modulates cognitive and non-cognitive components of behavior throughout lifespan in mice
data.authors: Halloran J; Hussong SA; Burbank R; Podlutskaya N; Fischer KE; et al.; Galvan V

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Asked whether the lifespan-extending dose of rapamycin harms or helps the aging BRAIN. Reassuringly, it enhanced learning and memory in young mice, prevented age-related cognitive decline in old ones, and even reduced anxiety and depression-like behavior - linked to boosted brain monoamines. Cognitive benefit, not cost.
data.abstract_excerpt: Aging is, by far, the greatest risk factor for most neurodegenerative diseases. In non-diseased conditions, normal aging can also be associated with declines in cognitive function that significantly affect quality of life in the elderly. It was recently shown that inhibition of Mammalian TOR (mTOR) activity in mice by chronic rapamycin treatment extends lifespan, possibly by delaying aging {Harrison, 2009 #4}{Miller, 2011 #168}.

extracted_findings.effect: Chronic rapamycin modulates cognitive and non-cognitive behavior across the lifespan in mice
extracted_findings.dose: 2.24 mg rapamycin per kg body weight/day via rapamycin-supplemented chow (14 mg/kg food), ad libitum, for periods ranging from 8 to 40 weeks
